passages.text: But as you’re deciding on work arrangements for your engineering team, opinions aren’t going to cut it. You need data.

passages.text: The good news? There’s comprehensive research from Stanford, Gallup , and the Bureau of Labor Statistics that actually gives us some clarity. The findings are more nuanced than the shouty debate suggests, but there’s a pattern—trust, not location, drives productivity.

passages.text: As part of the broader return-to-office landscape in 2025 , the productivity debate has become central to decisions about where and how teams work. Let’s get into what the research actually says.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done

passages.text: Stanford found hybrid workers are just as productive as office workers, with 33% lower turnover . That’s significant. When you factor in the cost of recruiting and onboarding replacements, that’s real money.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Does the Research Actually Show About Remote Work Productivity?

passages.text: Nicholas Bloom’s multi-year study tracked the same workers over time instead of taking snapshots. The result? No productivity drop when remote work has the right support—the right tools, clear accountability, and outcome-based measurement.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Does the Research Actually Show About Remote Work Productivity?

passages.text: 76% of remote and hybrid workers report improved work-life balance according to Gallup. Three-quarters of your team getting tangible benefits. That’s not nothing.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Does the Research Actually Show About Remote Work Productivity?

passages.text: Organisations that invested in collaboration tools and outcome-based performance metrics are seeing 40% productivity gains in remote settings. The companies struggling? Still managing by looking over shoulders and counting hours.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Does the Research Actually Show About Remote Work Productivity?

passages.text: What makes the difference? Three things: trust between managers and teams, outcome-based measurement instead of time-based surveillance, and intentional communication frameworks. Miss any of those and your remote arrangement will struggle.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Does the Research Actually Show About Remote Work Productivity?

passages.text: Here’s the problem: only 54% of managers trust remote teams to be productive according to Gallup.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: Nearly half of all managers don’t believe their team is working unless they can see them. That’s a management problem, not a remote work problem. This trust gap drives many of the return-to-office mandates we’re seeing across the industry.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: The data backs this up. 88% of remote workers feel pressure to prove productivity. 64% keep their chat status green even when not working. Low trust creates performative availability instead of actual output.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: High-trust environments enable outcome-based measurement. You focus on deliverables, sprint velocity, code quality, project milestones. Low-trust environments drive surveillance and micromanagement. You get monitoring software, excessive check-ins, and people optimising for looking busy instead of being productive.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: Companies that build high-trust cultures drive substantial business impact with remote work. Companies that can’t build trust struggle no matter where people sit.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: Building trust takes time. You need to shift from evaluating hours worked to evaluating output delivered. You need clear accountability frameworks. You need consistent results that demonstrate remote teams deliver.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: Many managers struggle because they’re used to visual oversight. Walking past someone’s desk and seeing them at their computer feels like confirmation they’re working. It isn’t, but it feels that way. Outcome-based evaluation requires actually looking at results. Managing engineering teams in hybrid work environments requires intentional frameworks that build trust through transparency rather than surveillance.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: If you don’t trust your team to work without constant supervision, you’ve got a staffing or management issue. Changing physical location won’t fix it.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Does Trust Affect Remote Work Productivity More Than Location?

passages.text: The data on hybrid work shows stability. Gallup’s Q2 2025 research shows 51% of remote-capable employees work hybrid. That number has held steady since 2022. It’s a new baseline, not a temporary adjustment.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: Hybrid workers now spend 46% of their workweek in the office—about 2.3 days. That’s up slightly from 42% in 2022, but the pattern holds: most people split their time.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: The productivity comparison is interesting. Hybrid workers match office workers on output but show 33% lower turnover. Office workers? 39% say they accomplish less in the office because of socialising.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: Schedule autonomy matters. The percentage of employees who say their hybrid schedule is “entirely up to me” declined from 37% in 2024 to 34% in 2025. More companies are mandating specific office days instead of letting teams self-organise.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: Self-determined schedules outperform employer-mandated schedules on both satisfaction and retention. When you tell people exactly which days to come in, you’re optimising for management comfort instead of team effectiveness.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: Most workers prefer 2-3 office days per week, but companies typically require 3-4 days . This gap creates friction.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: The optimal split appears to be 2-3 office days for most tech teams. More important than the exact number is who decides. Teams that choose their own office days outperform teams following arbitrary mandates.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What’s the Difference Between Hybrid, Remote, and Office Productivity?

passages.text: The shift is from time-based metrics—hours worked, attendance, time at desk—to output-based metrics—what got shipped, quality of work, project milestones hit.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: For engineering teams, track sprint velocity, deployment frequency, code quality metrics, pull request throughput, and project completion rates. These are the DORA metrics high-performing teams already use: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and mean time to recovery.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: The predictable mistake: companies that can’t trust remote teams turn to surveillance software. This correlates with lower trust and negative outcomes. Monitoring activity isn’t measuring productivity—it’s signalling distrust.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?
passages.speaker: The predictable mistake

passages.text: Companies using workforce analytics tools had 20% higher productivity rates than those relying on traditional management methods according to Gartner . The difference? Analytics tools measure outcomes and identify inefficiencies. Traditional methods measure presence and assume correlation with productivity.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: Avoid basic measures like lines of code or raw ticket counts. These create perverse incentives.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: Establish a baseline. Track your team’s productivity metrics in the original environment, then measure the same metrics after implementing remote or hybrid work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: Track leading indicators alongside lagging ones. Engagement scores, collaboration frequency, and knowledge sharing predict future productivity. If those are trending down, you’ll see it in deliverables later.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: Pick metrics that align with your business goals, make them transparent, and evaluate everyone using the same standards regardless of location.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > How Do You Actually Measure Productivity for Remote Workers?

passages.text: 76% of remote and hybrid workers experience improved work-life balance. 61% experience less burnout or fatigue.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: The mechanism is straightforward. Most people commute at least an hour daily. Remote work gives that time back. They sleep better, exercise more, spend more time with family, and have more control over their day.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: Better wellbeing drives higher engagement. Higher engagement drives better retention. Companies offering flexibility see 25-35% turnover reduction .
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: But remote work can create burnout if you implement it poorly. Without clear boundaries, remote work becomes always-on work. Without the physical separation of office and home, some people struggle to disconnect.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: The difference is autonomy and boundaries. When people control their work hours and have clear expectations about availability, burnout decreases. When remote work means being available 24/7 because you’re “always home anyway,” burnout increases.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: 75% of caregivers say flexibility helps them manage work and home . Caregivers are a substantial portion of your team—people dealing with childcare, elder care, or other responsibilities that don’t fit 9-to-5 office schedules.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: The data on workers with disabilities is particularly stark. 63% prefer working remotely. 42% would consider leaving if forced back to office. For many people, remote work makes employment viable.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: The wellbeing benefits translate to performance. When people control their time, they produce better work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Impact Does Remote Work Have on Work-Life Balance and Employee Wellbeing?

passages.text: 84% of remote workers report feeling more productive , but nearly half run into collaboration challenges. Individual productivity often goes up while collaborative friction sometimes goes up too.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: The office provided spontaneous interactions. You’d overhear a conversation, jump in with a solution. Remote work requires being more intentional. You need documentation culture and structured collaboration time.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: The key is optimising your mix of synchronous and asynchronous work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: Optimise for synchronous communication inside teams, asynchronous communication outside teams . Engineers within a team should have overlapping hours for real-time collaboration. Communication between teams should default to asynchronous—detailed documentation, recorded meetings, written updates.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: Hybrid models can optimise for both. Use remote days for concentrated work. Use office days for workshops, planning sessions, architecture discussions.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: Over 40% of hybrid employees feel disconnected from fully remote teammates. This requires active management. Proximity bias can develop where office workers get more context and remote workers get left out. Building trust and productivity in hybrid teams means deliberately counteracting these patterns.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: Strong documentation drives down the number of meetings needed between teams. Innovation depends more on team practices than physical proximity. Psychological safety and experimentation culture drive innovation more than location.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > Does Remote Work Actually Hurt Innovation and Collaboration?

passages.text: The business case for flexibility is compelling.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: 67% of companies under 500 employees offer full remote work versus only 10% of Fortune 500 firms. Small companies worked out they could recruit from anywhere, not just their local metro. This gives them access to talent that would never relocate.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: Companies enforcing return-to-office mandates face 23% longer hiring timelines, pay $5,000-$15,000 more per hire, and access only 40% of the available talent pool.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: Remote job postings are 15-20% of available positions but attract 60% of all applications.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: Workers with hybrid schedules were 33% less likely to resign than full-time office workers. 76% of companies experience greater retention by allowing remote work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: The cost of replacing someone ranges from 50-200% of their annual salary. A third fewer departures is substantial money saved.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: RTO mandates correlate with talent loss. 80% of companies reported losing talent because of RTO mandates. High-performing employees are 16% more likely to have low intent to stay if they face an RTO mandate.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: High performers leave first because they have the most options. Tech companies with RTO mandates lose 15 percentage points of senior workforce share.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: Remote-first companies save $10,000-$15,000 per employee annually on office space, utilities, and facilities. Even hybrid arrangements let you right-size office space, typically reducing space needs by 50-70%.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: Only 10% of Fortune 500 companies have achieved full return-to-office despite 83% of CEOs predicting this outcome. The gap between executive expectations and actual outcomes reflects current RTO trends and talent market dynamics.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > What Business Outcomes Can You Expect from Different Work Arrangements?

passages.text: It depends on how you implement it, not just location. Stanford’s hybrid study found equal productivity with 33% better retention. Success requires trust, proper measurement, and intentional collaboration frameworks. 56% of employees who prefer remote work report being more productive at home.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Is working from home really more productive than working in an office?

passages.text: Focus on output-based metrics instead of surveillance. Track deliverables, sprint velocity, code quality, and project milestones. Surveillance tools correlate with lower trust and negative outcomes, while outcome-based measurement drives better performance.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > How do I know if my remote employees are actually working?

passages.text: Gallup research identifies this trust gap as the main barrier. Managers accustomed to visual oversight struggle with outcome-based evaluation. Building trust requires shifting from time-based to output-based metrics, establishing clear accountability, and demonstrating consistent results over time.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Why do only 54% of managers trust remote workers?

passages.text: Research suggests 2-3 office days per week optimises collaboration benefits while maintaining flexibility. More importantly, self-determined schedules outperform employer-mandated schedules significantly. Give teams autonomy in choosing their office days based on collaboration needs.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > What’s the best schedule for hybrid work – two days, three days, or what?

passages.text: Yes. RTO mandates correlate with increased talent loss, especially high performers with in-demand skills. 80% of companies reported losing talent because of RTO mandates. High-performing employees are 16% more likely to have low intent to stay if they face RTO mandates.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Will return-to-office mandates make my company lose top performers?

passages.text: Less burned out. 76% report improved work-life balance in remote/hybrid arrangements. 61% experience less burnout or fatigue. Burnout risk decreases with autonomy, clear boundaries, and right-to-disconnect policies. It increases when remote work means always-on expectations without boundaries.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Are remote workers more burned out or less burned out than office workers?

passages.text: Collaboration changes rather than necessarily declining. Spontaneous collaboration decreases, but planned collaboration can improve with intentional frameworks. Hybrid models optimise both: deep focused work remotely, collaborative sessions in office. Documentation culture becomes critical.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Should I worry about collaboration suffering with remote work?

passages.text: Bureau of Labor Statistics data shows no systematic productivity decline with properly implemented remote work. Stanford research found productivity parity for hybrid arrangements. Organisations with collaboration tools and outcome-based metrics see 40% productivity gains in remote settings.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > How much productivity am I losing by letting people work from home?

passages.text: Shift from time-based metrics (hours worked) to output-based metrics (deliverables completed). Use sprint velocity, code quality, deployment frequency, project milestone completion, and customer satisfaction. Track engagement and collaboration as leading indicators of future productivity.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > What metrics should I use to measure remote worker productivity?

passages.text: 67% of companies under 500 employees offer full remote work versus only 10% of Fortune 500 firms. Remote-first companies save $10,000-$15,000 per employee annually. Companies offering flexibility see 25-35% turnover reduction. Workers with hybrid schedules were 33% less likely to resign.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Do companies with remote work really grow faster than office-only companies?

passages.text: Positive impacts include eliminated commute stress (1+ hour daily returned), better sleep, more family time, and improved physical health. Negative risks occur without boundaries or with always-on expectations. 76% of remote/hybrid workers report improved work-life balance. 61% experience less burnout.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > How does working from home affect employee mental health?

passages.text: Innovation depends more on team practices than physical proximity. Intentional collaboration frameworks, psychological safety, and documentation culture drive innovation. 84% of remote workers report feeling more productive, but nearly half face collaboration challenges requiring deliberate solutions.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work vs Office Productivity – What Research Actually Shows About Where Work Gets Done > FAQ Section > Is my team less innovative because they’re working remotely?

passages.text: The productivity debate around remote work isn’t simple, but the research points to a clear pattern: outcomes depend more on trust and management practices than physical location. As the return-to-office landscape continues to evolve, the evidence suggests that flexible work arrangements can deliver strong productivity when implemented with outcome-based measurement, intentional collaboration, and high-trust cultures.

passages.text: The debate about productivity in office vs remote work intensified after the global shift to distributed work models. Many organizations initially assumed productivity would decline when employees worked outside a centralized workplace. Data collected over the last several years shows a more complex reality.

Multiple studies indicate that employees working remotely often maintain or improve productivity. In fact, research shows 77% of remote workers report higher productivity levels, while employers also report stable or increased output from distributed teams.
However, the relationship between location and productivity is not linear. Productivity outcomes depend on several factors:

Organizations that attempt to compare remote and office productivity using simple output metrics frequently overlook these factors. Measuring productivity requires visibility into how teams actually work.

Workplace analytics platforms like Worklytics help organizations analyze collaboration patterns, meeting behavior, and digital activity to identify what truly drives productivity across work environments.
Remote work significantly changes how employees structure their workday. Several structural advantages explain why many knowledge workers report higher productivity when working remotely.

Studies indicate that remote workers spend less time being unproductive compared with office employees, largely due to reduced distractions.
Deep work requires sustained attention. When employees can control their work environment, they can allocate longer uninterrupted blocks of time to complex tasks.

Hybrid productivity reports show that remote workers can achieve up to 18.5 hours of deep focus per week, significantly higher than office-based employees.

Remote work allows employees to align their working hours with their most productive periods. Some professionals produce their best work early in the morning, while others perform better in late afternoon or evening.
Research indicates that 64% of employees report better focus when they have flexible working hours.
Flexible scheduling reduces cognitive fatigue and allows employees to plan their workload around periods of peak concentration.
Organizations that measure focus patterns using workplace analytics tools can identify when productivity peaks occur across teams.

Platforms like Worklytics enable organizations to analyze focus blocks, helping identify the sources of workflow fragmentation and allowing teams to protect the time needed to produce their most valuable work.
Commuting consumes time that could otherwise be used for productive work or recovery. Eliminating long commutes improves both productivity and well-being.
Employees often reinvest commute time into work or personal routines that support focus. In many cases, workers begin their day earlier and maintain higher energy levels.
Remote work also reduces stress associated with commuting logistics, which can influence cognitive performance and decision-making.

Worklytics provides insights into employee well-being indicators, helping companies detect overwork patterns and unhealthy meeting loads across distributed teams.

These advantages typically relate to collaboration quality and leadership visibility rather than individual task output.

passages.text: Editor’s note: This article was originally published in 2020 and updated in 2025 to include new research and findings from 2024. The original study remains below for context and comparison.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis

passages.text: Remote work isn’t new, but it is evolving. With millions still working outside traditional offices, questions about productivity, culture, and collaboration continue to shape the future of work. That’s why we revisited our original research with fresh 2024 data, analyzing responses from millions of employees across industries.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis

passages.text: Spoiler: Remote work still works. But how it works best is shifting — it all comes down to culture, trust, and leadership.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis
passages.speaker: Spoiler

passages.text: In this updated post, we’ll walk you through our latest findings, compare them to our earlier research from 20 19 –202 0 , and share what leading companies are doing now to sustain performance and engagement.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis

passages.text: As of February 2025, Gallup’s ongoing tracking of hybrid work arrangements in the U.S. found that 52% of U.S. employees whose jobs can be done remotely work in a hybrid environment.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study

passages.text: Another 27% are fully remote. That’s 79% of employees spending at least some of their time working remotely — a significant enough percentage to shape how organizations operate.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study

passages.text: In early 2024, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 34 to 35.5 million people aged 25 and older worked from home for pay , up 5 million from the previous year. This underscored a continued shift toward remote work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study

passages.text: In 2024, a sweeping analysis of Trust Index™ Survey data covering 1.3 million employees at Great Place To Work® Certified™ firms revealed a fascinating truth: Cooperation stands out as the cornerstone of discretionary effort , a defining trait of outstanding productivity.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study > T eam cooperation — not proximity — drives remote productivity

passages.text: Employees who feel they can count on others to cooperate are 8.2 times more likely to give extra effort.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study > T eam cooperation — not proximity — drives remote productivity

passages.text: But do teams need to be co-located to cooperate? Not at all.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study > T eam cooperation — not proximity — drives remote productivity

passages.text: Of the companies on the 2025 Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For® , 97 support remote or hybrid work . This study included 67,000 employees. And 84% of employees at these companies say they can count on colleagues to cooperate , compared to 65% in typical workplaces.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study > T eam cooperation — not proximity — drives remote productivity

passages.text: Employees at the Fortune 100 Best Companies don’t just show up — they show up strong. Productivity is nearly 42% higher at these companies compared to a typical U.S. workplace.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study > T eam cooperation — not proximity — drives remote productivity

passages.text: That extra drive shows up in all the right places: higher productivity, better customer service, stronger retention, and more agility when things shift.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > 2024–25 remote productivity study > T eam cooperation — not proximity — drives remote productivity
passages.speaker: That extra drive shows up in all the right places

passages.text: While our data shows strong and sustained productivity in remote environments, Gallup’s recent research adds nuance: High engagement doesn’t always mean high well-being.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: Gallup’s latest “ State of the Global Workplace” r eport found that fully remote workers report the highest engagement (31%) compared to hybrid (23%) and on-site workers (19%). But they also report lower well-being and higher instances of stress, anger, and loneliness.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: The paradox?
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: Autonomy boosts productivity, but it can also increase cognitive load and emotional strain . Leaders should support social interaction, structure, and mental health alongside flexibility.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: At high-trust workplaces, such as those found on the 100 Best Companies list, this paradox diminishes significantly due to exemplary leadership.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: In our 2025 Fortune 100 Best survey, 81% of employees at these companies described their workplace as psychologically and emotionally healthy — a stark contrast to the 45% reported in typical U.S. workplaces.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: This 45% higher rating underscores how strong leadership and intentional support create an environment where productivity and well-being thrive.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work paradox: When engagement rises but well-being falls

passages.text: Historical data shows that working from home can be just as productive, if not more so, than traditional office setups. In 2022, Great Place To Work's two-year study of more than 800,000 employees found stable or improved productivity after transitioning to remote work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Does remote work increase productivity?

passages.text: In 2020, we surveyed 715 companies representing over 3 million U.S. employees. We measured productivity through responses to statements about effort and adaptability:
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Does remote work increase productivity?

passages.text: People are willing to give extra to get the job done
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Does remote work increase productivity?

passages.text: People quickly adapt to changes needed for their company’s success
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Does remote work increase productivity?

passages.text: In the 2019–20 productivity study, we ran a comment analysis of employee survey responses to the open-ended question, “Is there anything unique or unusual about this company that makes it a great place to work?”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: Interestingly, the most common phrase among people experiencing high productivity changed over time. In March to May of 2020, the most common phrase was “ catered lunches at home , ” indicating the power of perks for increasing employee well-being and productivity.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: However, from June to August 2020, the most common phrase was “ genuinely love. ” Examples of these comments include:
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: “We are genuinely loved here!”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: “I have never been so genuinely loved and cared for by a workplace. I truly feel connected to my co-workers, and they’re one of the best parts of my day.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: “They are welcoming and open. Everyone that I talk to genuinely loves to be here every day, and that makes the hard stuff easier!”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: From September to December of that year, “ positive atmosphere ” was the most used phrase by employees to describe what makes their company a great place to work.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: While perks may have bolstered employee productivity during the early months of working from home, camaraderie and a positive culture influenced longer-term productivity.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: “Camaraderie is like a secret weapon. When employees experience the nexus of great work, a powerful mission, and shared values, productivity soars,” explained Julian Lute, Great Place To Work strategic advisor.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: “Employees in great workplaces believe their co-workers see them as whole people, with family, hobbies, and passions that they bring to work each day. When relationships are strong, employees feel energized and bring their skills to the table to collaborate on organizational goals.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Employee sentiment among productive remote workplaces

passages.text: Other unique phrases among employees who worked productively while remote were about leadership:
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: “ excellent leadership ” and “ outstanding leadership ” from March to May
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: “ incredible leadership , ” “ culture leadership , ” and “ leadership understands ” from June to August
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: “ incredible leadership ” and “ honest leadership ” from September to December
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: Such comments reveal how much impact leadership can have on employee productivity. And amid the pandemic and all its uncertainty, the power of great leadership was on full display.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: “When times are tough, leaders have the greatest opportunity to build trust. Their ability to navigate the complexities of the business, communicate effectively, and bring people along is more visible,” said Julian.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: “Consistent communication and supporting people in shifting work arrangements, all while taking care of customers, is a balancing act. But leaders who are vulnerable help employees to experience the workplace as supportive and caring.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Strong leadership is key to maintaining productivity and employee well-being

passages.text: Despite the initial increase, productivity fell in the summer of 2020, declining sharply from May to August by 11 percentage points (see graph).
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: However, by September, productivity began to pick up slightly, rising to 80% in December 2020 from its lowest point of 76% in August.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: Employees who dipped in summer may have had a spring of “toxic productivity” — an unhealthy compulsion to work, perhaps out of fear of layoff or a loss of work–life balance amid lockdown. And toxic productivity almost always comes from the top.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: Between June and August — the least productive months — the comment “ Hire leaders ” was repeated most by unproductive employees under survey questions about what could make the workplace better.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: For example:
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: “ Hire leaders that are NOT top performers – they are not leaders, they are performers. There’s a difference. We need to start hiring leaders and people who can coach and motivate.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: “We need to hire leaders that have experience. We should choose experience over friends any day, but that doesn’t always happen.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: “ Hire leaders throughout the company with more backbone who are willing to stand up for employees and pay people what their time is worth, not just the bare minimum.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: “Train and hire leaders , not bosses.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: “Employees expect their leaders to lead, make decisions and support their work,” said Julian.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: “Leaders who do not prioritize trust contribute to uncertainty, inconsistent communication, and lack of collaboration during challenging times. People expect their leaders to be guides and help them understand the broader business environment.”
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: Read more about the importance of trustworthy managers during a crisis .
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Why poor leadership kills remote work productivity

passages.text: In short: The early productivity drivers of remote work are now table stakes. Today, it’s your culture, leadership, trust and listening strategy that make the difference.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Remote work productivity: then vs. now
passages.speaker: In short

passages.text: Trust drives output. When employees feel safe, seen, and supported, they show up with more energy and initiative.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 1. Build a c ulture of t rust and c ooperation

passages.text: Be transparent early and often. Leaders who openly share updates — especially the messy, in-progress ones — build credibility.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 1. Build a c ulture of t rust and c ooperation

passages.text: Model cooperation. Try cross-functional “ask me anything” sessions. They boost alignment and make collaboration feel like the norm, not a hurdle.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 1. Build a c ulture of t rust and c ooperation

passages.text: Example: At Salesforce, the company holds regular “Ohana Meetings” where employees from different departments can ask questions and share updates. This practice has helped break down silos and foster a culture of transparency and cooperation.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 1. Build a c ulture of t rust and c ooperation
passages.speaker: Example

passages.text: Clear beats constant. Remote teams don’t need more Zooms — they need better clarity and flow.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 2. Make c ommunication e asy, n ot e xhausting

passages.text: Check in, not check up. Weekly one-on-ones or async video updates can do more for alignment than back-to-back meetings.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 2. Make c ommunication e asy, n ot e xhausting

passages.text: Keep the human in remote. Dedicated Slack channels for random musings, pet pics, or weekend recaps go a long way in keeping team spirit alive.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 2. Make c ommunication e asy, n ot e xhausting

passages.text: The best tools are the ones people actually use.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 3. Give t hem t ools t hat a ctually h elp

passages.text: Choose wisely, not excessively. Pick collaboration platforms that suit your team’s workflow — and don’t overwhelm them with five apps that do the same thing.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 3. Give t hem t ools t hat a ctually h elp

passages.text: Make access easy. Set up a central hub or doc with logins, FAQs, and SOPs so no one’s hunting for info.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 3. Give t hem t ools t hat a ctually h elp

passages.text: Example: At DHL Express, the “ Smart Connect ” intranet serves as a comprehensive hub, uniting 116,000 employees worldwide through streamlined access to local news, company policies, strategic updates, and HR tools.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 3. Give t hem t ools t hat a ctually h elp
passages.speaker: Example

passages.text: Designed to bridge operational and office divisions, the platform delivers content in local languages and offers personalized self-services, including payroll, attendance systems, job portals, and learning platforms.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 3. Give t hem t ools t hat a ctually h elp

passages.text: Beyond its practical functions, Smart Connect fosters a sense of community with social walls enabling employees — from the CEO in Florida to couriers in Malaysia — to share stories, photos, and videos, embodying the company’s #AsOne ethos.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 3. Give t hem t ools t hat a ctually h elp

passages.text: Let people work how they work best.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 4. Flexibility isn’t a perk — It’s a productivity multiplier

passages.text: Evidence from our report, “ Return-to-Office Mandates and the Future of Work ,” underscores a critical truth: mandating where employees work dampens productivity , whether onsite or remote. Conversely, when individuals or teams tailor policies to their needs, the result is striking — more employees are willing to go the extra mile.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 4. Flexibility isn’t a perk — It’s a productivity multiplier

passages.text: The statistics are telling. Fewer workers subject to rigid mandates report exerting discretionary effort, regardless of location. Flexibility, it appears, nurtures not only autonomy but also commitment. By granting employees the freedom to choose how and where they work best, organizations unlock a potential that rigid policies often stifle.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 4. Flexibility isn’t a perk — It’s a productivity multiplier

passages.text: Offer flexible hours: A 9-to-5 mindset doesn’t always make sense across time zones or energy peaks.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 4. Flexibility isn’t a perk — It’s a productivity multiplier
passages.speaker: Offer flexible hours

passages.text: Give autonomy : The more ownership you hand over, the more initiative you’ll see in return.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 4. Flexibility isn’t a perk — It’s a productivity multiplier
passages.speaker: Give autonomy

passages.text: Example: Australian-American proprietary software company Atlassian also supports flexibility through its “ Team Anywhere ” policy. It lets employees choose where to work each day, leading to a significant increase in applications and retention.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 4. Flexibility isn’t a perk — It’s a productivity multiplier
passages.speaker: Example

passages.text: Because it is. Burnout doesn’t show up on spreadsheets — until it does.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 5. Prioritize well-being like i t’s a business metric

passages.text: Normalize real breaks. Encourage calendar blocking for deep work and protect “off” time like you would a client meeting.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 5. Prioritize well-being like i t’s a business metric

passages.text: Support beyond work. Mental health stipends or open-access wellness resources show you actually mean it.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 5. Prioritize well-being like i t’s a business metric

passages.text: Example: Intuit’s approach to hybrid work harmonizes the rhythms of in-office and remote productivity, enriching its physical spaces with the essence of local art and cuisine. The well-being of employees is not merely acknowledged but celebrated through an expansive benefits package.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 5. Prioritize well-being like i t’s a business metric
passages.speaker: Example

passages.text: This includes home office reimbursements, access to mental health counseling, on-site fitness facilities, and a “ Well-Being for Life ” reimbursement valued at $1,300. Intuit also fosters a culture of vitality by championing healthy habits, rewarding them through the Virgin Pulse wellness program.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 5. Prioritize well-being like i t’s a business metric

passages.text: Recognition fuels momentum.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 6. Celebrate progress — big or small

passages.text: Make shoutouts a habit. Try “wins of the week” in team chats or highlight reels in all-hands meetings.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 6. Celebrate progress — big or small

passages.text: Create feedback loops. Let employees know what’s working — and how they’re contributing to the bigger picture.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 6. Celebrate progress — big or small

passages.text: Example: Ally Financial Inc. goes all in on recognition through initiatives like “BRIEFally” and “LEADing the Way,” spotlighting teammates who live the company’s values. Whether in-person or virtual, Ally ensures employees are celebrated through weekly shoutouts in newsletters and annual leadership awards.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 6. Celebrate progress — big or small
passages.speaker: Example

passages.text: This approach highlights not just what they achieve but how they do it. Recognitions like these boost morale while reinforcing the company’s “Do it Right” mission — empowering employees to carry their impact forward.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 6. Celebrate progress — big or small

passages.text: Innovation doesn’t just happen — it’s invited.
passages.heading_path: Remote Work Productivity Study: Surprising Findings From a 4-Year Analysis > Best practices for boosting productivity in remote teams > 7. Keep growing — together
